clients.description: Operations director at Calderbrook Freight, a haulage and logistics firm in Leeds. Married with two teenage children. Wants to consolidate four deferred workplace pensions into a single SIPP and review the family's life cover before his 50th birthday.

Partner at Kestrel & Lowe LLP, a family law practice in Manchester. Divorced in 2024; wants to rebuild her pension after the financial settlement, use her full ISA allowance each year and update her will.

Plumber and sole director of Stonebridge Plumbing & Heating Ltd in Bristol. Pays himself a small salary plus dividends and wants to start employer pension contributions through the company and build an emergency fund.

Retired primary school headteacher living in Cheltenham. Widowed; draws a Teachers' Pension and a small annuity. Wants to make regular gifts to her four grandchildren and reduce the inheritance tax due on her estate.

Consultant anaesthetist with the NHS in Leeds who also does private sessions at a clinic in Harrogate. Has exceeded the pension annual allowance and needs advice on the taper, Scheme Pays and her NHS Pension.

Runs Clarke & Finch, a branding studio in Brighton, with her business partner. Sold part of her shareholding to a larger agency in 2025 and wants to put some of the proceeds into her pension and the rest into a general investment account.

Known to everyone as Bill. Recently retired aerospace engineer from Derby and a deferred member of the Brackley Aero Engines pension scheme. Weighing up a transfer against taking the scheme pension and tax-free lump sum, and how to pay for care for his wife.
Founder and CTO of Quillstack, a Cambridge software start-up. Holds EMI share options and some vested shares; expects a sale of the company within two years and wants to plan for capital gains tax.

Pharmacist who owns two community pharmacies in Leicester. Executor of her late father's estate: the grant of probate came through in October 2025 and she now needs to sell his house in Loughborough and invest what she inherits.

Retired GP from Fort William. Moved her ISAs away from Glen Wealth Partners in 2023 because of high fees. Climbs Ben Nevis every June to raise money for the mountain rescue team and wants to leave them a legacy in her will.

queries.why: Assignment example: the term is John Doe's e-mail domain; his documents never mention it, so they are only acceptable (the query identifies him through his e-mail), while Morag Campbell, whose description mentions Ben Nevis and Glen Wealth Partners, is a trap for searches that split the word.

Assignment example: John Doe's utility bill and Jane Smith's council tax bill are the standard UK proofs of address although neither says 'proof' or 'address', the bank statement is a secondary option, and the courier 'proof of delivery' quoting his home address is a trap that must not be returned, let alone ranked first.

Document type named in the assignment example: only the Brightwell Energy bill is a utility bill, the council tax bill is a close household bill and acceptable, while Bill Hargreaves (nickname in his e-mail and description) and the bank statement are not what was asked for.
The usual UK wording of the assignment's 'address proof' must give the same answer; the courier note contains all three words ('proof of delivery', 'home address') but is still a trap.
All-lowercase form of the assignment example; the example itself already requires case-insensitive matching of 'NevisWealth' against a lowercase e-mail.
Upper-case form of the assignment example (caps lock left on); letter case must not change the answer.

A full e-mail address typed with capitals must match the stored lowercase address; his documents are acceptable because the query identifies him, but not required because none of them contains the address.
The assignment example with a trailing question mark, which must be ignored rather than break the query or change the answer.

The client record must come first, and his utility bill, passport, P60 and letter of authority all name John Doe in their text, so they are required too; the courier note only says 'J. Doe' and is acceptable as part of his file.
Leading, trailing and repeated spaces must be collapsed, so the answer is identical to 'John Doe'.

Jane Smith's record first plus her passport, council tax bill and consent order, which name her; the will notes only say 'Jane' and are acceptable as her own file, while Oliver Smith, the invoice from 'Mr Smith' and Janet Smyth are different people and wrong.
Double quotes must be stripped or treated as a phrase; every relevant record contains the exact phrase 'Jane Smith', so the answer is the same as without quotes.
Surname first with a comma, as names appear in many back-office lists; neither the comma nor the word order may change the answer.
First name only: Jane Smith and every document whose text says 'Jane', including the will notes; Janet Smyth and her passport only share the prefix 'Jane' and are a different person.

Surname only: both Smith clients and every document naming a Smith (the invoice's 'Mr Smith' is Oliver); Smyth is a common variant spelling, so Janet Smyth and her documents are acceptable, and Jane's will notes are acceptable as part of a matched client's file.

Name plus document type: Jane Smith's passport must be first; her client record and other documents are acceptable, but John Doe's passport and the passport of the similarly named Janet Smyth are exactly the wrong answers.
Name plus document type: the P60 names John Doe and must be first; his client record and his other documents are acceptable, nothing else is.

Accented name typed as stored: client first plus both documents that name her; the bank statement spells her 'Siobhan' without the fada, so accent-insensitive matching is needed, hence expected rather than required.
Accent removed, as most UK keyboards type it: must still find the client stored as 'Siobhán' and the pension statement that uses the fada, as well as the bank statement spelt without it.
Typographic apostrophe (U+2019) pasted from Word or Outlook must be treated like the straight apostrophe stored in the corpus.
No accent and no apostrophe, as in her e-mail address: the client matches through the e-mail, and the two documents that write 'O'Connell' should still be found by folding the apostrophe.
Accent added relative to the share purchase agreement, which spells her 'Zoe Clarke': the client (stored as Zoë) comes first and the agreement must also be found.
Full legal name: the client first and his transfer value statement, which names him; Morag Campbell's record and letter of wishes mention Fort William, a different-field trap for the word 'William'.

Nickname: the client is found through 'Bill' in his e-mail and description and must be first; his transfer value statement says 'William Hargreaves' and is acceptable, while the utility bill and council tax bill share only the word 'bill' and are wrong.

His only document, the Quillstack shareholder register, never names him, so it is not required, but it is acceptable because the query names its owner; Priya Raman's record and the grant of probate share only the word 'grant' and are wrong.
The grant of probate document must be first and Priya Raman's description mentions the grant, so both are required; Grant Whitfield is a first-name trap.

Employer named in John Doe's description, his P60 and letter of authority, and in Oliver Smith's invoice to the firm, so all four are relevant; John Doe's passport, utility bill and courier note never mention it and are wrong, because a description-only match does not pull in the owner's unrelated documents.

City in two client descriptions and in four documents' addresses (the courier note is relevant here because it really contains a Leeds address), while the same clients' documents that never mention Leeds (passport, letter of authority, NHS statement) are wrong.

Firm in Jane Smith's description and e-mail domain and in her will meeting notes; her other documents do not mention it and are only acceptable, because the query also matches her e-mail (the same rule as for NevisWealth).
The hyphenated form from her e-mail domain must also find the meeting notes, where the firm is written 'Kestrel & Lowe'.
Start-up named in Grant Whitfield's description and e-mail domain and in its own shareholder register, so both the client and the document are required.
Occupation found only in Siobhán O'Connell's description; her pension statement and bank statement do not mention it, so returning them for a description-only match is noise and counts as wrong.
Appears only in Morag Campbell's description; her letter of wishes does not mention it and is wrong, and John Doe's 'neviswealth' e-mail is a substring trap.
An exact e-mail looks up one client, who must be first; her share purchase agreement does not contain the address, so it is acceptable as her file but not required.

Life event in Jane Smith's description; the consent order and will notes say 'divorce', the same term in another form, so they are required, while her passport and council tax bill are unrelated and wrong.

Janet Smyth's description, her record of gifts and the grant of probate all deal with inheritance tax; Priya Raman administers the estate on which it was paid and is acceptable, while Morag Campbell's charity legacy does not mention the tax and is wrong.

A postcode search wants every document showing that address, so here the courier note is relevant alongside the utility bill; John Doe (whose record holds no address) and his other documents are acceptable as the person who lives there, while other Leeds postcodes are wrong.

National Insurance number typed without the spaces used in the P60 ('QQ 12 34 56 C'); spacing-insensitive identifier matching is a nice-to-have, and John Doe and his file are acceptable as the person it identifies.
Grant Whitfield's description says 'start-up' and the missing hyphen must not matter; the shareholder register after a seed round is acceptable as a start-up document although it never uses the word.
Written 'tax-free' in both Bill Hargreaves's description and his transfer value statement; the missing hyphen must not stop the match.
Keyboard-mash junk with no meaning: nothing in the corpus is what the adviser wants, so a fuzzy or semantic search must not pad the list with nearest neighbours.
A real place that appears nowhere in the corpus; Morag Campbell is Scottish but lives in Fort William, so no client or document is about Edinburgh.
No client called Michael Brown exists; John Doe's passport contains his middle name Michael, but a full-name search that returns a different person is wrong.
Classic SQL injection: it must be treated as plain text and, since no record contains 'or' or '1' as a word, return nothing rather than every row (and never a 500).
Stacked-statement injection: it must stay harmless text that matches nothing (no record contains 'drop', 'table' or 'clients'), and both tables must still be intact afterwards.
Script injection in the query: nothing matches, and the API must answer with a JSON array rather than echo the markup back unescaped.

A lone SQL LIKE wildcard must be escaped: no record contains a per-cent sign (amounts are written 'per cent'), so the answer is empty and never the whole corpus; rejecting it with 400/422 as a query without searchable text would also be tolerable.

queries.q: Hi, quick one before Thursday: could you pull up the copy of Jane Smith's passport and the latest council tax bill we hold for her? Compliance have flagged that her identity and address checks need redoing because the passport scan is from January and the bill must be less than three months old. If either is missing let me know so I can chase her directly. Thanks
queries.why: A pasted colleague e-mail: the adviser wants exactly Jane Smith's passport and council tax bill; her record and other documents are acceptable, while John Doe's and Janet Smyth's passports, the utility bill and the courier note matched on single words are wrong (natural-language understanding is a nice-to-have).

queries.why: About 1,500 characters of nonsense words: the API must cope with a very long query (no 414 or 500) and, as nothing matches, return an empty list.
Emoji only: multi-byte non-Latin input must not crash the search, and it matches nothing, so the answer is empty.

http_cases.why: Happy path with every field: 201 Created with the stored Client, including its new id, echoed back (the wording shares no term with any search query).
Only the three required fields: description and social_links are optional, so the client must still be created.
first_name is required: a validation error, never 201 or 500.
last_name is required: a validation error, never 201 or 500.
email is required: a validation error, never 201 or 500.
email has format email, so a string without an '@' must be rejected.
An explicit null is not a string, so a required name cannot be null.
description must be a string; a number is the wrong type and should be rejected, not silently coerced.
social_links must be an array of strings; a single bare string is the wrong type.
Every element of social_links must be a string, and 42 is not.
Truncated, unparseable JSON sent as the raw body: 400 is the REST convention and 422 is what FastAPI-style validators return; never 500.
The body must be a single JSON object, not an array of clients.
POST without any body: a validation error (400/422), or 415 if the server insists on a JSON content type; never 201 or 500.

body.title: Ongoing advice fee agreement
body.content: Signed agreement for ongoing advice at 0.75 per cent a year of assets under advice, invoiced quarterly in arrears.

http_cases.why: Happy path: c10 is the corpus client Morag Campbell (substitute her real id); 201 with the Document including id, client_id, title, content and a server-set created_at, worded to avoid every search query term.
title is required for a document: a validation error, never 201 or 500.
content is required for a document: a validation error, never 201 or 500.
title must be a string; a number is the wrong type.
Truncated JSON for a document body: 400 by REST convention or 422 from schema validators; never 500.

No client 999999 exists: 404 is the REST answer for a missing parent (400/422 only if this id format is itself invalid for the API); 201 would create an orphan document and 500 means a foreign-key error leaked.
The same check with a well-formed but non-existent UUID for APIs that use UUID ids: 404 expected, 400/422 only if UUIDs are not the id format; never 201 or 500.
q is required: omitting it is a validation error, not a 200 with an empty list or with every record.
An empty q carries no search text; a required parameter must not be empty (OpenAPI disallows empty values by default), so reject it rather than answer 200.
Whitespace-only q is empty once trimmed and must be rejected like an empty q rather than sent to the engine, where a vector search would return arbitrary nearest neighbours.
Happy path: 200 with a JSON array (containing John Doe, c01).
A NUL byte in q (PostgreSQL text cannot store it) must be stripped or rejected with 400/422; it must never surface as a 500.
